## Web Development Company in Pune: How to Plan Your Website Structure and Navigation Before Development Starts

Before a web development company in Pune writes any code, you should hand it a structure document: a list of every page the site needs, the URL each page will live at, how those pages connect in the navigation, and which search phrase or customer question each page exists to answer. Decide this first and design, development and content writing become faster and cheaper. Skip it and the structure gets decided implicitly, by whichever template the developer happens to start from, and you discover the gaps only after launch, when a service has no page and the menu has eleven items.

This article is for owners and marketing leads who are commissioning a new website or replacing an old one. It covers how to build a page inventory, how to design URLs and navigation, how to map keywords to pages, how to split service pages from blog posts, what XML and HTML sitemaps are for, how to protect your existing search visibility with a redirect map, and how a developer should actually use the document you produce. A worked example follows, using a clearly hypothetical firm. You do not need technical knowledge, and you can do most of the work in a spreadsheet.

## Why a web development company in Pune needs your structure first

Most website briefs start with look and feel: colours, a reference site you like, a homepage banner. Those matter, but they sit on top of a structure. If the structure is wrong, no amount of visual polish repairs it, because the problem is that visitors and search engines cannot find or understand what you offer.

Structure decides three practical things.

- **Whether visitors find what they came for.** A buyer looking for "CNC job work" who has to guess that it lives under "Capabilities, then Machining, then Other" will leave.
- **Whether search engines can match pages to queries.** A search engine ranks pages, not websites. If three services share one page, that page competes weakly for all three. If each has its own page, each can answer one query properly.
- **What the project costs.** Page count, templates and features drive development effort. A structure document turns "a website for my company" into a countable scope, which is what makes quotes comparable. Our guide to [twelve questions to ask before requesting a quote](/blog/web-development-company-pune-shortlist-questions-2026) assumes you can describe your scope; this document is how you do that.

Changing structure after development is expensive in a specific way. Moving a page means changing its URL, its menu position, every internal link pointing to it, and the redirect from the old address. Doing that on a spreadsheet costs minutes. Doing it on a built site costs developer hours and risks broken links.

## Step 1: Build the page inventory

A page inventory is a flat list of every page the new site will contain. Start with a spreadsheet and these columns: page name, purpose, primary audience, main call to action, content status (exists, needs rewriting, needs creating) and owner (who supplies the content).

Work through four sources to fill it.

1. **Your offering.** One row per distinct service, product line or programme that a customer could buy or ask about separately. Test: could a customer plausibly search for this on its own? If yes, it earns a page.
2. **Your trust material.** About, team or leadership, certifications, case studies or portfolio, testimonials, client list where permitted, facilities.
3. **Your conversion pages.** Contact, request a quote, book a call, brochure download, careers if you hire, and any thank-you pages that confirm a form submission.
4. **Your legal and utility pages.** Privacy policy, terms, cookie notice where relevant, and a custom 404 page. If you collect personal data through forms, the privacy notice is not optional, and [the DPDP Act compliance article](/blog/dpdp-act-website-compliance-pune-2026) explains what the page and your forms need to cover.

If you are replacing an existing site, add a fifth source: export the current URL list (from the CMS, a crawl or your existing XML sitemap) and from analytics note which pages get traffic and which get enquiries. Pages with traffic or inbound links from other sites are assets, even if the content is poor. Pages with neither can usually be merged or dropped.

### Page types, not just pages

Group the inventory into page types, because a type becomes one template in development. Typical types for a business site are home, hub or category pages (such as Services), detail pages (one per service), proof pages (case studies), editorial pages (articles), conversion pages (contact, quote request) and utility pages (privacy, 404). A site with forty pages usually has only six or seven templates, and counting templates rather than pages is the more honest way to estimate design and development effort.


## Step 2: Design URL structure

URLs are addresses, and good ones are boring: short, readable, lowercase, hyphen-separated, and reflecting where the page sits in the site. Google's own guidance is that URL structure should be simple and logical, and that descriptive words help people as well as crawlers.

Rules that hold up in practice:

- **Mirror the hierarchy, but not too deep.** `/services/cnc-machining` is clear. `/what-we-do/capabilities/machining/cnc/cnc-machining-services` is a maintenance burden.
- **Use words your customer would use.** `/services/website-creation`, not `/services/svc-01`.
- **Keep them stable.** The best URL is one that never changes. Avoid dates in URLs for evergreen content, and avoid including a year in a service page address, since you will want to update the page without moving it.
- **One canonical form.** Decide on trailing slash or none, `www` or non-`www`, and HTTPS only, and have the server redirect every other variant to the chosen one.

A rule of thumb for depth: a visitor should reach any page within three clicks of the homepage, and the URL should rarely exceed two path segments for service pages. Blog posts are the exception, since they are many, and a flat blog folder with one level of post names is easier to maintain than nested category folders.

## Step 3: Plan the navigation

Navigation is the visible form of your structure. It answers "what is here, and where do I go next" in under five seconds.

**Main menu.** Five to seven top-level items is a sensible ceiling. More than that and visitors skim past everything. Order by what a first-time visitor needs, not by internal org chart: services or products first, proof next, then about, then contact. Make contact a visually distinct button rather than one more text link.

**Drop-downs.** Use them where a hub has many children (services, industries), and keep them one level deep. Mega-menus are justified for large catalogues, but on a thirty-page company site they usually signal that the structure has not been simplified. On touch devices a drop-down needs to be tappable, so confirm that the hub page itself is a real, useful page, not just a menu label.



**Internal links in the body.** Menus are not the only links. Service pages should link to related services and to relevant proof; articles should link to the service page they support. These contextual links often carry more meaning than the menu, because the anchor text describes the destination.


## Step 4: Build a keyword-to-page map

A keyword map assigns each important search phrase to exactly one page, so that your pages support each other rather than compete. It is a small table, and it is the single most useful input a developer or SEO specialist can receive.

Columns: target phrase, the question behind it (informational, comparing options, ready to buy), the page assigned, page type, and notes on what the page must contain.

How to build it:

1. **List what you sell in customers' words.** Use enquiry emails, sales call notes and WhatsApp messages. The phrases your customers use are often not the ones in your brochure.
2. **Check what the results page looks like.** Search the phrase in an incognito window. If results are dominated by service pages from companies like yours, a service page is the right format. If they are guides and comparisons, you need an article. If a map pack appears, location signals and a Google Business Profile matter more than page copy; see [our local search explainer](/blog/local-seo-google-map-pack-pune-2026).
3. **Assign one primary phrase per page.** Related phrases can sit on the same page as secondary terms, but two pages should not target the same primary phrase. When they do, you get what is called cannibalisation: two of your own pages splitting the signals.


## Service pages versus blog posts

A frequent structural mistake is putting everything in the blog or putting nothing in it. The two formats do different jobs.

| | Service or product page | Blog article |
|---|---|---|
| Reader's state | Ready to evaluate or buy | Learning, comparing, solving a problem |
| Query shape | "web designer Pune", "CNC job work" | "how to choose...", "what does X cost" |
| Main goal | Enquiry or purchase | Trust, and routing the reader to a service page |

Plan the connection explicitly. Each service page should have a small set of supporting articles that answer the questions buyers ask before they enquire, and each article should link up to the service page it supports. This is sometimes called a topic cluster, but the plain version is enough: a page that sells, surrounded by pages that help. Google's documentation on [creating helpful, reliable, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) is a good yardstick for whether an article deserves to exist.


## XML sitemap versus HTML sitemap

These two are often confused, and they serve different readers.

**XML sitemap.** A machine-readable file, usually at `/sitemap.xml`, listing the URLs you want search engines to know about. It helps crawlers discover pages, particularly new ones or those with few internal links. Google's [sitemap documentation](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/sitemaps/build-sitemap) states that a single sitemap is limited to 50MB uncompressed or 50,000 URLs, that larger sites must split into several files with a sitemap index, and that Google ignores the `priority` and `changefreq` values. It uses `lastmod` only if it is consistently and verifiably accurate, so a developer who sets every page to today's date on every build is making the field useless.


**HTML sitemap.** A normal page for people, listing the major sections of the site as links. On a small site it is optional. On a larger site with many services, industries or resource pages, it works as a fallback for visitors who are lost, and as an extra internal route to deep pages. Link it from the footer. Do not treat it as a substitute for sound navigation; if you need it to make the site usable, the navigation is the problem.


## A worked example: a hypothetical Pune precision-engineering firm

To make this concrete, consider a fictional company, "Example Precision Works", a mid-sized machining and fabrication business in a Pune industrial area. It is invented for illustration; none of the numbers or details describe a real client.

Its old site has twelve pages built over several years. The "Services" page lists CNC machining, fabrication, tooling and quality inspection in a single block. There are two competing "About" pages. The product photos sit in PDFs. Enquiries come mostly through phone and WhatsApp, and the contact form is a bare email link.

**The brief for the new site.** The company wants more enquiries from procurement managers in automotive and general engineering who are comparing job-work suppliers in the Pune region.

**Page inventory (excerpt):**

| Page | Type | Primary audience | Main action |
|---|---|---|---|
| Services (hub) | Hub | Procurement, engineers | Pick a service |
| CNC machining | Detail | Procurement | Request a quote |
| Fabrication | Detail | Procurement | Request a quote |
| Capabilities and machine list | Proof | Engineers | Download capability sheet |
| About and certifications | Trust | Vendor-approval teams | Contact |
| Blog hub plus six launch articles | Editorial | Researchers | Read, then go to a service |
| Contact and quote request | Conversion | Everyone | Submit form |
| Thank-you page | Utility | Form submitters | None |
| Privacy policy, 404 | Utility | Everyone | None |


**URLs (excerpt):** `/services/cnc-machining`, `/services/fabrication`, `/industries/automotive`, `/capabilities`, `/case-studies/bracket-redesign` (a placeholder name), `/insights/how-to-qualify-a-job-work-supplier`.

**Navigation:** Services (drop-down with four items), Industries (drop-down with two to start), Capabilities, Case Studies, About, and a Request a Quote button. Six items, one level of drop-down, contact set apart as a button.

**Keyword map (excerpt):**

| Target phrase | Intent | Assigned page |
|---|---|---|
| CNC machining job work Pune | Ready to buy | /services/cnc-machining |
| sheet metal fabrication Pune | Ready to buy | /services/fabrication |
| how to qualify a machining supplier | Researching | Blog article, links to the CNC page |
| vendor approval documents for components | Researching | Blog article, links to About and certifications |

The reasoning shows the point. The two ready-to-buy phrases get their own pages, each in the main menu. The researching phrases go to articles that route readers upward. Nothing shares a primary phrase.


## Redirect mapping when you replace an existing site

If the old site has any search visibility, links from other sites or bookmarked pages, a redirect map is part of the structure work, not an afterthought. Without it, every old URL that no longer exists returns a not-found error, and the value those pages had is lost.

Build it as a table with three columns: old URL, new URL, redirect type. Method:

1. **Collect every old URL.** Combine the CMS export, a crawl, the old XML sitemap, Search Console's performance report (pages that received impressions) and analytics landing pages. Backlink data, if you have access to it, shows pages that other sites link to.
2. **Map each to the closest new equivalent.** The closest match is the page that answers the same need. Mapping everything to the homepage is poor practice; Google treats mass redirects to irrelevant pages like soft not-found errors, and visitors are confused.
3. **Use permanent redirects (301 or 308)** for pages that have moved for good. Google's [redirect documentation](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/301-redirects) explains the types and states that permanent server-side redirects are the right choice when a URL changes.
4. **Avoid chains.** Old A to old B to new C wastes crawl effort and slows visitors. Point A directly to C.
5. **Allow genuine removals.** If a page has no equivalent and no value, let it return a 404 or 410 and make sure the 404 page offers a path onward.
6. **Test before launch.** Run the whole list against the staging site, then again immediately after launch. Fix anything that does not return the expected result.

If you are weighing whether to rework the current site or start over, our comparison of [website redesign versus rebuild](/blog/website-redesign-vs-rebuild-pune-2026) will help you decide before the structure work starts.


## How a developer should use the structure document

The document is a working specification, not a presentation. A competent team uses it in these ways.

- **Scoping and quotation.** Pages, templates, special features (filters, calculators, downloads, multilingual versions) and integrations become the line items. Two vendors quoting from the same inventory are quoting the same thing.
- **URL and redirect implementation.** The URL column becomes routing rules; the redirect map becomes server configuration.
- **Acceptance testing.** At the end, the inventory is the checklist: does every page exist, at the right URL, in the right menu position, with its keyword in the title and heading, and does every link resolve?

For this to work, version the document. Put a date and revision in the file name, and require that changes after sign-off go through a written change request, since a late "can we add an industries section" changes templates, content and cost.

## Common mistakes

- **One "Services" page for everything.** It cannot rank for or properly answer several different queries.
- **Duplicate or near-duplicate pages.** City-name swaps and repeated service descriptions dilute rather than add.
- **Forgetting the redirects.** The most expensive mistake on a replacement, and the cheapest to prevent.

## A pre-development structure checklist

Use this before you sign off on development.

1. Every page is listed with type, audience, purpose and call to action.
2. Templates are counted, and each is named.
3. Every URL is written out, lowercase, hyphenated, no deeper than two levels for services.
4. Main menu has seven or fewer items; contact is a button.
5. Every important phrase is assigned to one page, and no two pages share a primary phrase.
6. Each service page has at least two supporting articles planned.
7. XML sitemap rules are agreed (what is included and excluded); HTML sitemap decision made.
8. Redirect map is complete for every old URL with traffic, links or enquiries.
9. Content owners and dates are assigned for every page.
10. Change requests are defined in writing.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How many pages should a small business website have?

There is no correct number; the right count is the number of distinct things a customer might search for or need to know, plus trust, conversion and legal pages. Many small business sites work well with 10 to 30 pages. Add a page when it answers a separate question, and avoid padding with near-duplicates.

### Do I need an HTML sitemap if I already have an XML sitemap?

Usually not on a small site. The XML sitemap is for search engines, and the HTML sitemap is for people. An HTML sitemap is a useful fallback on larger sites with many sections, but it is no replacement for clear navigation.

### Should my blog be on the same domain as my main website?

In most cases yes, as a folder such as /blog, so the articles and the service pages they support sit in one site and can link to each other naturally. Splitting the blog onto a separate domain or subdomain makes it harder for the articles to support your service pages.

### What happens to my Google rankings if I change my website's URLs?

If you redirect every old URL to its closest new equivalent with permanent redirects, the pages can carry over most of their search standing, though a temporary fluctuation is normal. If you skip the redirects, old pages return errors and you can lose the visibility and links they had. Build and test the redirect map before launch.

### How deep should website navigation go?

Aim for any important page within three clicks of the homepage, and keep drop-down menus to one level. Deep nesting hides pages from visitors and weakens the signals to search engines about which pages matter.
